intro: Some of the most famous secret society documents in the world were never secret and never real. A satire about a French emperor was rewritten into a hate forgery. Typed pages were slipped into a national library to invent a medieval order. An anonymous roll of film offered a top secret committee no agency had ever formed. A British television spoof about a plan to leave Earth was later repeated as a real exposé.

These fakes matter because people believed them, and some did great harm. The Protocols of the Elders of Zion was used to spread hatred of Jews for decades and was promoted by the Nazi state. In this unit you will put the people who were harmed, and the people who exposed the lies, at the center of the story.

You will also learn the historian's tools. You will compare texts in parallel columns, trace claims back to their origin, and test documents by provenance, material, anachronism and who gains. You will study one real find, the Chinon Parchment, to see that a surprising document can be genuine. By the end, you will be able to test a document yourself and explain your verdict with evidence.
bigQuestion: How do we prove a document is forged or genuine, and why do some proven fakes keep spreading?

choices: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail

It described a secret Jewish meeting
test.why: Joly's satire was about Napoleon III and does not mention Jews at all.

test.why: Graves was The Times correspondent in Constantinople in 1921.

choices: Proof that one text was built from another, shown by shared wording, images and order
A reader's need for a dictionary
A code used by secret societies
test.why: Shared wording, images and order in the same sequence show that the newer text depends on the older.

test.q: Which is still debated about the Protocols?
test.why: Historians agree it is a forgery copied from Joly, but they still debate who the forger was.

test.q: What did the Bern court find on 14 May 1935?
test.why: Judge Walter Meyer found the Protocols to be forgeries and trashy literature.

test.q: Why did Henry Ford's support make the Protocols more dangerous in America?
choices: He had proven it true in court
His fame lent the forgery credibility it had not earned
test.why: Readers trusted Ford because of his success, which had nothing to do with the text's truth.

test.q: Which statement about Ford's 1927 apology is accurate?
choices: It stopped every copy of The International Jew
Ford later took it back in court
It was drafted by Louis Marshall and signed by Ford after the Sapiro mistrial
test.why: Louis Marshall drafted it, and Ford signed it on 30 June 1927 after the Sapiro trial ended in a mistrial.

test.q: What gave the Dossiers Secrets a false look of authority?

test.why: Being deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale made the pages look official, though the library does not certify contents.

test.q: How did the MJ-12 papers first appear?

test.q: Why did many viewers miss that Alternative 3 was a spoof?

It was aired only in French
The government said it was true

test.q: How does the Chinon Parchment show that a surprising document can be real?

It was found in a national library in 1967
test.why: Unlike the planted papers, the parchment passes provenance, material and consistency tests.

test.q: A post shares a passage from the Protocols but says it is about the Illuminati. What should a careful reader conclude?

It is harmless because no group is named
It must be true because it keeps being reprinted
It is still the same forgery, with its origin in Joly and its history of harm unchanged
test.why: Renaming the villain does not change where the text came from or what it was made to do.

title: Forgeries and Fakes

chapters.title: The Protocols: Anatomy of a Forgery
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a careful reader prove that a document is a forgery, and why can a proven lie keep doing harm?

story.title: An Old Book in Constantinople
story.kicker: In 1921 a British reporter is handed a worn French book and finds the famous secret plan already inside it.
paragraphs: It is the summer of 1921 in Constantinople, the great city on the Bosporus now called Istanbul. Philip Graves is the correspondent there for The Times of London. The city is crowded with people who fled the Russian Revolution and civil war. Some of them bring stories. Some bring papers. One of them brings Graves a book.

The man is a Russian exile. In his articles Graves calls him only Mr. X. Historians later identified him as Mikhail Raslovlev. He hands over an old French book, worn from use, and says something strange. Read this, he tells Graves, and then read the Protocols of the Elders of Zion.

Graves knows the Protocols. It is a pamphlet that claims to be the secret minutes of Jewish leaders plotting to rule the world. It has spread across Europe and America since the Russian Revolution. Many readers treat it as proof of a hidden plot. Even in Britain, some serious people have asked whether it might be real.

Graves reads the French book. It is a satire from 1864, written by a lawyer named Maurice Joly to mock a French emperor. It does not mention Jews at all. Yet page after page, its ideas and images match the Protocols, often in the same order. Graves begins to set the two texts side by side. In August 1921 The Times prints what he found.
story.think: Graves had a strong hunch, but he did not just announce it. Why was printing the two texts side by side more convincing than simply saying the Protocols were fake?

lessons.title: Joly's Satire of 1864
lessons.mainIdea: The Protocols copied a French satire from 1864 that attacked Emperor Napoleon III and never mentioned Jews.
reading: In 1864 a French lawyer named Maurice Joly published a book in Brussels, Belgium. He did not put his name on it. The title page said only that it was written by a contemporary, meaning someone living at the time. Its title in English is Dialogue in Hell Between Machiavelli and Montesquieu.

The book is a *satire*. A satire uses humor, irony or exaggeration to criticize real people or real power. Joly's target was Napoleon III, the emperor of France. Joly believed the emperor kept a free-looking government on the surface while controlling it underneath. He could not safely say that openly, because France had strict *censorship*, meaning government control over what could be printed.

So Joly wrote a *dialogue*, a text written as a conversation. Two dead thinkers argue in the afterlife. Montesquieu defends laws, liberty and a free press. Machiavelli explains, coldly and cleverly, how a modern ruler could control newspapers, courts and voters while pretending to respect them. Readers were meant to recognize Napoleon III in Machiavelli's plans.

The French government did recognize him. Joly was identified, tried and sentenced in April 1865 to 18 months in prison. His book was seized and soon forgotten. Keep one fact in mind for the rest of this chapter: Joly's satire is about a French emperor. It does not mention Jews at all.

words.d: writing that uses humor, irony or exaggeration to criticize real people or real power
government control over what may be printed, said or shown
a piece of writing set out as a conversation between speakers

look.title: Joly's Book, as the Catalog Records It
look.text: A dialogue in hell between Machiavelli and Montesquieu, or the politics of Machiavelli in the nineteenth century, by a contemporary. Printed in Brussels by A. Mertens and Sons, 1864.
look.cite: Maurice Joly, Dialogue aux enfers entre Machiavel et Montesquieu, Brussels: A. Mertens et fils, 1864 (title page, in English)
look.prompt: The title page does not name the author, and the book was printed outside France. What do these two choices suggest about the risks Joly faced?

check.q: Who was the real target of Joly's 1864 satire?
check.why: Joly wrote the Dialogue to criticize Napoleon III; readers were meant to see the emperor in Machiavelli's plans.

check.q: Why did Joly write his criticism as a conversation between two dead thinkers?
choices: Because he wanted to write a history of Italy
Because Montesquieu had asked him to
Because France had strict censorship and open criticism was risky
Because the book was meant for children
check.why: France controlled the press, so Joly hid his attack inside a satirical dialogue. He was still jailed for it.

check.q: Which statement about Joly's book is true?
choices: It describes a secret Jewish meeting
It never mentions Jews at all
It was first printed in Russia in 1903
It was praised by Napoleon III
check.why: Joly's satire is about a French emperor and does not mention Jews. That fact matters when we compare it to the Protocols.

lessons.title: A Forgery Appears in Russia
lessons.mainIdea: The Protocols was first printed in a St. Petersburg newspaper in 1903 and in a fuller book version in 1905.
reading: Nearly forty years after Joly's book, a new text appeared in the Russian Empire. In August and September of 1903, a St. Petersburg newspaper called Znamya, meaning The Banner, printed it in parts. The paper's editor was Pavel Krushevan, a writer known for his hostility toward Jews. The text later became known as the Protocols of the Elders of Zion.

A *protocol* here means the official minutes of a meeting. The text claims to be the secret minutes of Jewish leaders planning to take over the world. It is a *forgery*: a document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive. No such meeting took place, and no such leaders existed.

In 1905 a religious writer named Sergei Nilus printed a fuller version as the last chapter of a book of his. Nilus's edition became the one most often translated. The timing matters. The Russian Empire was a place of deep *antisemitism*, meaning hatred of or prejudice against Jews. In those years mobs carried out deadly attacks on Jewish communities, called pogroms. A forgery like this did not create hatred from nothing. It fed on fears that already existed and gave them the look of proof. That is why historians study not only who wrote a false document, but also who wanted to believe it.

words.d: here, the official written minutes of a meeting
a document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive
hatred of, or prejudice against, Jewish people
a violent mob attack on a Jewish community, especially in the Russian Empire

look.title: From Satire to Forgery: Key Years
look.cite: Joly (1864); Znamya, St. Petersburg (1903); S. Nilus (1905); P. Graves, The Times, 16-18 Aug. 1921
look.prompt: How many years passed between Joly's satire and the first printing of the Protocols? How might that gap have helped the forgers?

check.q: Where was the Protocols first printed?
choices: In The Times of London in 1921
In a St. Petersburg newspaper in 1903
check.why: The reading says Znamya, a St. Petersburg paper edited by Pavel Krushevan, printed it in 1903.

check.q: In this chapter, what is a forgery?
choices: A true record that was later lost
A satire that openly mocks a ruler
A translation of an older book
A document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive
check.why: A forgery is made to deceive. The Protocols pretends to be secret minutes of a meeting that never happened.

check.q: According to the reading, why did the Protocols find believers in the Russian Empire?
choices: It fed on antisemitic fears that already existed
It was signed by famous leaders
It was sold as a comic novel
The government had tested it in court
check.why: The reading says the forgery fed on existing hatred and gave it the look of proof.

lessons.title: Who Made It? An Open Question
lessons.mainIdea: Historians agree the Protocols is a forgery, but they still debate exactly who made it.
reading: Students often ask who wrote the Protocols. The honest answer is that historians are not sure. There is a difference between two questions. Is the text a forgery? That question is settled. Who forged it? That question is still open, and historians argue about it using evidence.

The traditional view points to the Okhrana, the secret police of the Russian tsar, and its office in Paris. The historian Norman Cohn, in his 1967 book Warrant for Genocide, followed this view, which rests partly on witnesses who spoke at a trial in the 1930s. In 1999 a Russian scholar, Mikhail Lepekhin, named a writer called Mathieu Golovinski as the author. That claim is disputed.

Other historians look elsewhere. Cesare De Michelis, in a 2004 study, argued that the text came from Russian nationalist circles around 1902 and 1903. Scholars also agree that the forger borrowed from more than one source. One was an 1868 German novel by Hermann Goedsche, which included an invented scene of a secret meeting in a Prague cemetery.

This is a good example of how a *historian* works. A historian studies the past using evidence and says how sure each claim is. We can hold two ideas at once. We know the Protocols is fake because of what it copies. We do not yet know for certain whose hands did the copying. An open question about the author does not reopen the question of the forgery.

words.d: the secret police of the Russian tsars before 1917
a person who studies the past using evidence and says how sure each claim is
a claim about who made or wrote something

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim A: The Protocols copies long passages from Joly's 1864 satire. Claim B: The Russian secret police in Paris produced the Protocols. Claim C: Mathieu Golovinski wrote the Protocols. Claim D: The Protocols records a real secret meeting of Jewish leaders.
look.prompt: Label each claim as settled by evidence, still debated by historians, or shown false. For one claim, name the evidence that decides it.

check.q: Which question about the Protocols is settled?
choices: Which office of the secret police paid for it
check.why: The reading says that the forgery is settled, while the identity of the forger is still debated.

check.q: What did Cesare De Michelis argue in 2004?
choices: That the text came from Russian nationalist circles around 1902 and 1903
That Joly wrote the Protocols himself
That Graves invented the whole story
check.why: De Michelis argued for Russian nationalist circles, a different view from the traditional secret police account.

check.q: Besides Joly, which other source did the forger borrow from, according to scholars?
choices: An 1868 German novel by Hermann Goedsche
check.why: Scholars agree that Goedsche's 1868 novel, with its invented Prague cemetery scene, was also used.

lessons.title: The Times Prints the Proof
lessons.mainIdea: In August 1921 Philip Graves showed in The Times that the Protocols had been copied from Joly's satire.
reading: Philip Graves was a careful British journalist based in Constantinople. After Mr. X gave him Joly's book, Graves compared it with the Protocols line by line. He found that the Protocols had borrowed Joly's arguments, images and order of ideas. The forger had changed the speaker. In Joly, it is Machiavelli advising a ruler. In the Protocols, it is the supposed Jewish elders.

The Times printed Graves's findings in three articles on 16, 17 and 18 August 1921. The paper then reissued them as a pamphlet with a plain title: The Truth About the Protocols: A Literary Forgery. A *literary forgery* is a fake that is built by copying and changing someone else's writing.

This mattered because of who was speaking. The Times was one of the most respected newspapers in the world. The year before, some voices in Britain had asked whether the Protocols might be genuine. Now the same paper laid out the *evidence* for readers to judge. Evidence is the facts or documents that show whether a claim is true. Graves did not ask readers to trust him. He showed them the two texts together. That choice turned a debate about opinions into a test anyone could check with their own eyes.

words.d: a reporter who sends news from a particular place, often abroad
a fake text built by copying and changing someone else's writing
facts or documents that show whether a claim is true

look.title: What Graves Reported
look.text: Graves reported that the Protocols was largely a clumsy copy of Joly's 1864 satire on Napoleon III. The forger kept Joly's arguments and their order, and replaced the French emperor's methods with a supposed Jewish plan.
look.cite: Philip Graves, The Truth About 'The Protocols': A Literary Forgery, from The Times (London), 16, 17 and 18 August 1921
look.prompt: Graves's finding has two parts: what was kept and what was changed. Why are both parts important for proving a forgery?

check.q: When did The Times print Graves's articles?
check.why: The reading gives 16, 17 and 18 August 1921 as the dates of the three articles.

check.q: What did the forger change when copying Joly?
choices: The language, from Russian to French
The speaker, from Machiavelli to supposed Jewish elders
The ending, so that Montesquieu wins
check.why: Graves showed that the forger kept Joly's arguments but put them in the mouths of invented Jewish elders.

check.q: Why did it matter that The Times published this exposure?
choices: It was the only paper in Constantinople
It owned the rights to Joly's book
It was run by the Russian government
It was a respected paper, and some voices in Britain had taken the Protocols seriously
check.why: The reading says The Times was widely respected, which gave the evidence a large and serious audience.

lessons.title: Reading in Parallel Columns
lessons.mainIdea: Setting two texts side by side lets any reader see copied structure, wording and order.
reading: Graves used a simple tool: *parallel columns*. He printed a passage from Joly on one side and the matching passage from the Protocols on the other. Readers could move their eyes back and forth. They did not need to know French or Russian history. They only needed to compare.

What should a reader look for? First, the order of ideas. Two authors writing on their own might share one idea, but they will rarely share twenty ideas in the same order. Second, distinctive images, such as an unusual comparison or example. Third, small leftovers: details that made sense in the original but look odd in the copy.

This lesson uses an invented, harmless example so the method is clear. In the practice below, one text is an original school newsletter and the other copies it. You will not read the Protocols itself. That text was written to spread hatred. Historians who teach it show only short matching lines, and only to prove the copying. When a match is long, detailed and in the same order, chance is not a reasonable explanation. The newer text depends on the older one. That is called *textual dependence*. It is one of the strongest kinds of proof a historian can offer.

words.d: two texts printed side by side so readers can compare them line by line
proof that one text was built from another, shown by shared wording, images and order
unusual enough to stand out and be recognized

look.title: Practice: Two Newsletters
look.text: Original (a school newsletter, March): Our garden is a small country. The tomatoes are its citizens, the fence is its border, and the hose is its only road. Copy (a flyer found in April): The club is a small country. Its members are its citizens, its rules are its border, and the hose is its only road.
look.prompt: List three things the flyer kept from the newsletter. Which leftover detail gives the copy away, and why does it look odd in the new text?

check.q: What are parallel columns?
choices: Columns of numbers in a budget
Two texts printed side by side for comparison
check.why: Graves printed Joly and the Protocols side by side so readers could compare them line by line.

check.q: Why is the same order of many ideas strong evidence of copying?
choices: Because two independent authors rarely share many ideas in the same sequence
Because all authors write in the same order
Because order is the only thing a forger cannot change
Because courts only accept evidence about order
check.why: The reading says independent writers might share one idea, but rarely twenty in the same order.

check.q: In the practice flyer, which detail is a leftover from the original?
choices: The hose is its only road
check.why: A hose makes sense in a garden but not in a club, so it is a leftover from the newsletter being copied.

lessons.title: What the Copying Proves
lessons.mainIdea: Because the Protocols copies a satire about a French emperor, it cannot be the real record of a Jewish meeting.
reading: Proof of copying leads to a clear conclusion. Suppose the Protocols were real minutes of a secret meeting. Then the speakers' words would be their own. But the words are Joly's, written in 1864 to mock Napoleon III. A real meeting could not have produced a speech that already existed, word for word in places, in a French satire.

The copy also carries odd leftovers. Some are an *anachronism*, something placed in the wrong time. Scholars have noted passages that fit France under Napoleon III better than the world of 1903, because that is what Joly was writing about. A forger working fast did not clean every trace.

The deeper point is about blame. Joly's satire was a warning about how any ruler could abuse power. The forger took that warning and pinned it on a whole people who had nothing to do with it. That is what made the forgery so dangerous. It turned a general fear of power into hatred of a specific group. Notice what the proof does not need. It does not depend on who the forger was or on anyone's opinion of Jews. It rests on the texts themselves. Anyone can check it. That is why historians call the question closed.

words.d: something placed in a time where it does not belong
a person or group unfairly blamed for problems they did not cause
a judgment reached by reasoning from evidence

look.title: A Chain of Reasoning
look.text: Step 1: Joly's satire was printed in 1864 and attacks Napoleon III. Step 2: The Protocols first appeared in 1903. Step 3: Long parts of the Protocols match Joly in wording, images and order. Step 4: Therefore the Protocols depends on Joly.
look.prompt: Add a Step 5 that explains why the Protocols cannot be the real minutes of a secret meeting. Which step would a defender of the Protocols have to prove wrong?

check.q: What is an anachronism?
choices: A hidden message in a text
Something placed in a time where it does not belong
A second copy of a document
check.why: An anachronism is something out of its proper time, like details about Napoleon III's France in a text claiming to be from 1903.

check.q: Why can the Protocols not be the record of a real meeting?
choices: Because its words were already written by Joly in 1864 to mock a French emperor
Because it was first printed in Russian
Because no one read it before 1921
check.why: A real meeting could not produce speeches already written decades earlier in a satire about Napoleon III.

check.q: According to the reading, what made the forgery especially dangerous?
choices: It was written by a famous author
It turned a warning about any ruler into hatred of a specific people
It was hard to find in libraries
check.why: The forger pinned Joly's general warning about power on Jews, making them a scapegoat.

lessons.title: The Bern Trial
lessons.mainIdea: In 1935 a Swiss court in Bern ruled that the Protocols were forgeries, and a 1937 appeal did not change that finding.
reading: In the 1930s, pro-Nazi groups in Switzerland handed out copies of the Protocols. Swiss Jewish organizations went to court in Bern, the Swiss capital. They argued that the pamphlets broke a Bern law against trashy literature. The trial ran from October 1934 to May 1935, and witnesses testified about where the text came from.

On 14 May 1935, Judge Walter Meyer gave his ruling. He found the Protocols to be forgeries and called them trashy literature. Two of the five men charged, named Fischer and Schnell, were convicted. The other three were *acquitted*, meaning found not guilty.

The defendants made an *appeal*, asking a higher court to review the case. On 1 November 1937 the appeals court overturned the convictions. Its reason was a point of law: it held that the trashy literature statute did not fit a political text like this one. The appeals court did not rule that the Protocols were genuine. Later promoters of the Protocols sometimes say the Bern verdict was overturned, as if that proved the text real. That is a misreading. A *verdict* can be reversed because a law does not apply, while the facts found about a document still stand.

words.d: a court's decision in a case
found not guilty by a court
a request for a higher court to review a lower court's decision

look.title: The Bern Verdict, 14 May 1935
look.cite: Bern trial records, verdicts of 14 May 1935 and 1 November 1937 (EHRI archival description)
look.prompt: Only two of five men were convicted, and the appeal later overturned those convictions too. Does either fact tell us the Protocols might be real? Explain.

check.q: What did Judge Walter Meyer find in May 1935?
choices: That the Protocols were genuine minutes
That the Protocols were forgeries and trashy literature
That Joly had been a Russian spy
That the case should be sent to Russia
check.why: Meyer's verdict of 14 May 1935 found the Protocols to be forgeries and trashy literature.

check.q: Why did the appeals court overturn the convictions in 1937?
choices: It found new proof the Protocols were real
It held that the trashy literature law did not fit the text
check.why: The appeal turned on a point of law. The court did not find the Protocols genuine.

check.q: What does acquitted mean?
check.why: Acquitted means found not guilty. Three of the five men in Bern were acquitted in 1935.

lessons.title: Henry Ford's Newspaper
lessons.mainIdea: Beginning in 1920, Henry Ford's Dearborn Independent spread the Protocols to millions of American and foreign readers.
reading: Henry Ford was one of the most admired men in America. His Model T put millions of families on the road. He also owned a weekly newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, based in Dearborn, Michigan. On 22 May 1920 the paper began a series of attacks on Jews, and it kept them up in 91 more issues.

The series leaned heavily on the Protocols. It presented the forgery as a key to world events. The articles were then collected into books under the title The International Jew. The first volume appeared in November 1920. Ford's fame gave the old Russian forgery an American voice and a huge new audience.

This is a lesson about *propaganda*, meaning information spread on purpose to shape what people believe, often by misleading them. Propaganda works better when a trusted figure spreads it. Many readers reasoned that a man as successful as Ford must know what he was talking about. His success in business had nothing to do with whether the Protocols were true. The International Jew was translated into at least 16 languages, according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. It traveled far beyond Michigan, including to Germany, where Nazi leaders praised it.

words.d: information spread on purpose to shape beliefs, often by misleading people
a set of related articles printed one after another
the quality of being trusted and believed

look.title: Ford's Paper and the Forgery
rows: Series begins in the Dearborn Independent
look.cite: The Dearborn Independent (1920-1927); The Times (London), Aug. 1921; Ford statement of 30 June 1927
look.prompt: Graves's proof appeared in 1921. For how many years after that did Ford's paper keep running? What does this tell you about whether debunking alone stops a lie?

check.q: When did the Dearborn Independent begin its series attacking Jews?
check.why: The series began in the 22 May 1920 issue and ran in 91 more issues.

check.q: What is propaganda?
choices: A court ruling on a document
Information spread on purpose to shape beliefs, often by misleading
check.why: Propaganda aims to shape what people believe. Ford's series used the Protocols this way.

check.q: Why did Ford's name help the forgery spread, according to the reading?
choices: His fame and success made readers trust him, though that had nothing to do with the truth
He was a lawyer in the Bern trial
check.why: The reading says readers trusted Ford because of his success, which lent the forgery credibility it did not earn.

lessons.title: Ford's Apology of 1927
lessons.mainIdea: A libel suit pushed Ford to sign a public apology in 1927, but the books his paper made kept spreading.
reading: In the 1920s the Dearborn Independent also attacked Aaron Sapiro, a Jewish lawyer who organized farmers' cooperatives. Sapiro sued Ford for *libel*, meaning printing false statements that damage someone's reputation. The trial in 1927 ended in a mistrial. Before a new trial could begin, Ford decided to settle the matter.

Ford signed a public statement dated 30 June 1927. It was drafted by Louis Marshall, a leader of the American Jewish Committee, and Ford accepted it without changes. In it Ford apologized to Jewish people, said he withdrew the attacks, and said he had not known the details of what his paper printed. At the end of 1927 the paper stopped publishing.

Historians debate how sincere the apology was. Ford owned the paper, and many doubt he did not know what it said. Also, copies of The International Jew kept circulating abroad, especially in Germany. In 1938, on his 75th birthday, Ford accepted a high honor from Nazi Germany, the Grand Cross of the German Eagle.

A *retraction* is a public statement taking back something said or printed. Ford's retraction shows both the power and the limits of correcting the record. It was real and public. It did not recall the books already printed or the ideas already planted.

words.d: printing false statements that damage a person's reputation
a trial that ends without a verdict and may have to be held again
a public statement taking back something that was said or printed

look.title: Ford's Statement, in Summary
look.text: Ford said he regretted that his paper had been used to spread charges against Jews, apologized for the harm done, and promised the attacks would end. He said he had not known the details of what was printed.
look.cite: Henry Ford, public statement of apology, dated 30 June 1927, drafted by Louis Marshall of the American Jewish Committee
look.prompt: Ford owned and funded the paper. How believable is the claim that he did not know what it printed? What evidence would help you decide?

check.q: What pushed Ford toward his 1927 apology?
choices: Aaron Sapiro's libel suit against him
check.why: Sapiro's libel suit ended in a mistrial, and Ford signed the apology before a new trial.

check.q: Who drafted the statement that Ford signed?
choices: Louis Marshall of the American Jewish Committee
check.why: Louis Marshall drafted the statement, and Ford accepted it without changes.

check.q: Why do historians say the apology had limits?
choices: Copies of The International Jew kept circulating, and many doubt Ford's claim he did not know
It was printed only in Russian
check.why: The books kept spreading abroad, and historians question Ford's claim of ignorance about his own paper.

lessons.title: The Forgery in Nazi Germany
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi leaders used the Protocols as propaganda, helping build the hatred that led to the Holocaust.
reading: In Germany after World War I, the Protocols found eager readers among people looking for someone to blame for defeat and hard times. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazi writer Alfred Rosenberg introduced Adolf Hitler to the text in the early 1920s. The Nazi party published at least 23 editions of it between 1919 and 1939.

Some German newspapers fought back. In 1924 the Frankfurter Zeitung, a respected paper, exposed the Protocols as a fraud. But after the Nazis took power in 1933, independent voices were silenced. The Protocols was even used in some German schools. Once they took power, they could print it with the full weight of the state behind it.

The forgery gave Nazi *ideology* a false story of a hidden enemy. An ideology is a set of ideas that a movement uses to explain the world and justify its actions. The Nazi state used that story to justify taking away Jewish people's rights, property and safety.

The end of that road was the *Holocaust*, the murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during World War II. A forged document did not cause the Holocaust by itself. But historians see it as one of the lies that prepared many people to accept persecution. The people harmed, not the forgers, are the center of this history.

words.d: a set of ideas a movement uses to explain the world and justify its actions
the murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during World War II
cruel and unfair treatment of people because of who they are or what they believe

look.title: A Museum's Summary
look.text: The Holocaust Memorial Museum explains that the Nazis promoted the Protocols to justify persecuting Jews, publishing many editions and using it in some schools, even though it had long been exposed as a forgery.
look.cite: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Protocols of the Elders of Zion'
look.prompt: The forgery had been exposed in 1921 and again in 1924. Why might a government keep using a text it could know was fake?

check.q: Who introduced Hitler to the Protocols in the early 1920s, according to the museum?
check.why: The Holocaust Memorial Museum says Alfred Rosenberg introduced Hitler to the text.

check.q: Which German paper exposed the Protocols as a fraud in 1924?
check.why: The reading says the Frankfurter Zeitung exposed it in 1924, before the Nazis took power.

check.q: What is an ideology?
choices: A set of ideas a movement uses to explain the world and justify its actions
check.why: An ideology is a movement's set of explaining ideas. The Protocols gave Nazi ideology a false hidden enemy.

lessons.title: A Lie That Keeps Returning
lessons.mainIdea: Though proven false for over a century, the Protocols still circulates, sometimes with the villain renamed.
reading: In 1964 a subcommittee of the United States Senate Judiciary Committee printed a report on the Protocols. Its title called the text a fabricated historic document. Even at the height of the Cold War, members of Congress put on record that the Protocols was fake and traced how it had spread.

Yet the text never went away. It is still printed and still shared online in many languages today. Human rights groups and Holocaust museums continue to track it. A lie that has been disproved can keep moving if people pass it on without checking where it came from. That is called *misinformation* when it is shared by mistake, and *disinformation* when it is spread on purpose.

Sometimes the Protocols returns in a new costume. Some writers keep the text but say it is really about a different secret group, such as the Illuminati. The writer Bill Cooper reprinted it in his 1991 book Behold a Pale Horse, a case this course studies in Unit 17. Many of Cooper's readers care about real government secrets, and some of those secrets are documented.

But renaming the villain does not change the text's history. It is still Joly's satire, rewritten by a forger to target Jews, and still the document the Nazis used. A reader can take real questions about secrecy seriously and still refuse to pass on a known forgery.

words.d: false information shared by people who do not know it is false
false information spread on purpose to deceive
made up or invented, especially to deceive

look.title: Same Text, New Label
look.text: A post online shares a long passage and says: This old document explains everything about the secret elite who run the world. It gives no author, no date and no place of first printing. A reader notices that the passage matches, in order, a text historians traced to Joly's 1864 satire.
look.prompt: The post never names Jews. Does that make it harmless to share? Use the words disinformation and fabricated in your answer.

check.q: What did a U.S. Senate subcommittee do in 1964?
choices: It held that the Protocols were genuine
It printed a report calling the Protocols a fabricated document
It put Henry Ford on trial
check.why: The 1964 Senate Judiciary subcommittee print called the Protocols a fabricated historic document.

check.q: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
choices: Misinformation is always spoken; disinformation is always printed
Misinformation is shared by mistake; disinformation is spread on purpose
They mean exactly the same thing
Disinformation is true; misinformation is false
check.why: The reading defines misinformation as false information shared by mistake and disinformation as spread on purpose.

check.q: Why does renaming the villain not make the Protocols a different document?
choices: Because its history as Joly's satire rewritten to target Jews stays the same
Because Bill Cooper wrote the original
Because the Senate approved the new version
check.why: The reading says the text's origin and use against Jews do not change when the label changes.

lessons.title: Answering a Forgery With Care
lessons.mainIdea: The best answers to a hate forgery are checking its source, showing the evidence, and remembering the people it harmed.
reading: Graves, the Bern witnesses and the Frankfurter Zeitung reporters all did the same basic thing. They asked where the text came from and showed the answer. That is the heart of *source criticism*, the historian's habit of asking who made a document, when, where, how and why, before trusting it.

Careful people also avoid spreading the harm. Teachers who study the Protocols show only short matching lines next to Joly, and only to prove the copying. They do not hand out the full text. Repeating a hateful claim, even to argue with it, can plant it in new minds. Pointing to the evidence is safer than repeating the lie.

Center the people who were harmed. Jewish families in Russia, Germany and elsewhere lived with the fear and violence this text helped stir up. Honor also the people who stood up: Graves and his source, the Swiss Jewish groups who went to court, Louis Marshall and Aaron Sapiro in America, and the German reporters of 1924.

Finally, learn the pattern. Many forgeries follow the same shape: a secret meeting, a hidden group, a plan to rule the world, and no way to check the source. When you meet that shape, you can slow down, ask the source questions, and look for the original. That is a skill, and it grows with practice.

words.d: the habit of asking who made a document, when, where, how and why, before trusting it
the known history of a document: where it came from and who has held it
a shape or set of features that repeats across many cases

look.title: Five Source Questions
look.text: Who made this? When and where was it first printed? How did it reach me? Why might someone want me to believe it? Can I find the original, or an older text it copies? A student uses these five questions on a viral page that claims to reveal the secret minutes of a world meeting.
look.prompt: Which of the five questions would have exposed the Protocols fastest? Explain how Graves answered that question in 1921.

check.q: What is source criticism?
choices: Saying bad things about a writer
Copying a source into a report
Asking who made a document, when, where, how and why, before trusting it
Choosing only sources you agree with
check.why: Source criticism is the historian's set of questions about a document's origin and purpose.

check.q: Why do careful teachers show only short matching lines of the Protocols?
choices: Because the full text is lost
Because the goal is to prove the copying without spreading the hateful text
Because it is too hard to read
Because the law forbids any quotation
check.why: The reading says repeating hate can plant it in new minds, so teachers show only paired lines as proof.

check.q: Which set of features is the common pattern of such forgeries?
choices: A named author, a clear date and a library record
A court verdict and an appeal
A satire that openly names its target
A secret meeting, a hidden group, a plan to rule the world, and no checkable source
check.why: The reading lists this shape so readers can recognize it and slow down.

review.why: Joly's satire criticized Napoleon III and never mentioned Jews.

That Joly was guilty of libel
review.why: The appeal turned on a point of law and made no finding that the Protocols were real.

review.q: Henry Ford's 1927 apology came after which event?

review.why: Ford signed the apology after the Sapiro libel trial ended in a mistrial.

review.q: How did Nazi Germany use the Protocols?
choices: It banned the text as a forgery
It published many editions and used it as propaganda, even in some schools

review.why: The Holocaust Memorial Museum reports at least 23 Nazi editions and use in some schools.

review.q: A writer reprints the Protocols but says it is really about the Illuminati. What is the best response?
choices: It becomes a new, genuine document
It is harmless because Jews are not named

The text is still a forgery copied from Joly and used to target Jews
review.why: Renaming the villain does not change the text's origin or the harm it was made to do.

chapters.title: Planted Papers: Dossiers Secrets, MJ-12 and Alternative 3
chapters.bigQuestion: What tests can a historian use to tell a planted or invented document from a genuine one?

story.title: Pages No One Remembers
story.kicker: In 1967 a thin typed file about a secret priory enters France's national library, and a legend begins to grow from it.
paragraphs: Picture a cataloguer at the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris in the late 1960s. The national library holds millions of items. Every book and pamphlet printed in France is supposed to be deposited there. Most arrivals are ordinary. Some are strange.

One file is a set of typed and copied pages under the name Henri Lobineau. It is titled Dossiers Secrets, French for secret files. It contains family trees, notes and a list of the grand masters of a hidden order called the Priory of Sion. The list includes famous names such as Leonardo da Vinci and Isaac Newton.

No one on the staff recognizes the author. No scholar has ever mentioned this priory. Yet the file now has a library call number, and anything in the national library carries a quiet kind of authority. Later writers will say they found the secret in the Bibliothèque nationale, as if that alone proved it true.

The file was deposited on 27 April 1967. It was not a lost medieval record. It was a modern invention, planted so that it could be found. In this chapter you will meet three documents like it, one real document that looked just as unlikely, and the tests historians use to tell them apart.
story.think: Why might a forger want a fake document to be found in a famous library rather than simply printed as a pamphlet?

lessons.title: Pages Planted in a Library
lessons.mainIdea: The Dossiers Secrets were typed pages deposited in France's national library in 1967 to make an invented order look historic.
reading: The Dossiers Secrets d'Henri Lobineau entered the Bibliothèque nationale de France on 27 April 1967. A national library is the main library of a country. In France, publishers must send it copies of what they print. That rule is called *legal deposit*, and it means almost anyone can get a printed item onto the library's shelves.

The pages claimed that a secret society called the Priory of Sion had existed since the Middle Ages. They linked it to the Knights Templar and listed a line of grand masters, including Leonardo da Vinci and Isaac Newton. The file offered no medieval originals, no archive references and no way to check its claims.

The trick was about *authority*, the power to be believed because of who or what stands behind a claim. The library's catalog number made the pages look official. But a library records what it receives. It does not certify that the contents are true. The file had been *planted*: placed where it would later be found, so that finding it would seem like discovery. Historians call this a problem of provenance, the known history of where a document came from and who has held it. The Dossiers Secrets had a very short provenance. It began in 1967, with the people who deposited it.

words.d: a rule that publishers must send copies of what they print to a national library
the power to be believed because of who or what stands behind a claim
placed on purpose where it would later be found, to fool the finder
the known history of a document: where it came from and who has held it

look.title: What a Call Number Proves
look.text: A student finds an entry in a national library catalog. It gives a title, an author's name, a year and a shelf number. The student writes in a report: This document is in the national library, so its claims are true.
look.prompt: What does a library catalog entry actually prove about a document? Rewrite the student's sentence so that it claims only what the evidence shows.

check.q: When were the Dossiers Secrets deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale?
check.why: The reading gives 27 April 1967 as the date the file entered the national library.

check.q: What does legal deposit mean?
choices: A rule that publishers send copies of what they print to a national library
A court order to seize a book
A bank account for a library
check.why: Legal deposit is why almost any printed item can enter the national library, whether its claims are true or not.

check.q: Why did being in the library not prove the file was true?
choices: The library had lost the file
The file was written in Latin
A library records what it receives but does not certify its contents
Only books by famous authors are true
check.why: The reading says a library records what it receives and does not certify that the contents are true.

lessons.title: The Makers Confess
lessons.mainIdea: The men behind the Priory of Sion papers, Pierre Plantard and Philippe de Chérisey, later admitted the story was invented.
reading: The Priory of Sion was real in only one sense. In the 1950s a Frenchman named Pierre Plantard registered a small club by that name. It had no connection to the Middle Ages. Plantard, working with his friend Philippe de Chérisey, then produced documents to give the club an ancient past, with Plantard himself as a descendant of old French kings.

The Dossiers Secrets were part of that effort. So were parchments that were said to be medieval. De Chérisey later admitted that he had made the parchments himself. Like the Dossiers, they were *hoaxes*: tricks meant to make people believe something false.

The strongest evidence came from Plantard. In 1993 a French judge was investigating a separate matter in which Plantard's name came up. Under oath, Plantard admitted that his Priory claims had been invented. A *confession* is a person's own statement that they did something. A confession under oath, made to a judge, carries special weight in history as well as in law. So the Priory of Sion is a rare case in which the makers of a hoax told us, on the record, that they made it. Historians did not need to rely on guesswork. The claim that a medieval Priory guided the Templars is shown false.

words.d: a trick meant to make people believe something false
a person's own statement that they did something
after promising formally to tell the truth, as in a court

look.title: Weighing a Confession
look.text: Evidence 1: The Priory's own papers first appear in the 1960s. Evidence 2: No medieval record mentions the Priory. Evidence 3: De Chérisey says he made the parchments. Evidence 4: Plantard admits under oath in 1993 that his Priory claims were invented.
look.prompt: Rank these four pieces of evidence from strongest to weakest. Explain why a sworn confession by the maker might be stronger than the silence of medieval records.

check.q: Who created the Priory of Sion papers?
choices: Pierre Plantard and Philippe de Chérisey
check.why: The reading names Plantard and de Chérisey as the makers of the Priory documents.

check.q: What did Plantard admit under oath in 1993?
choices: That his Priory claims had been invented
That the Priory was founded in 1099
That Newton had been a member
That the library had stolen his papers
check.why: In a 1993 judicial inquiry, Plantard admitted under oath that the Priory claims were invented.

check.q: What is a hoax?
choices: A trick meant to make people believe something false
check.why: A hoax is a deliberate trick. The Priory parchments and Dossiers were hoaxes.

lessons.title: From Hoax to Bestseller
lessons.mainIdea: Popular books turned the Priory hoax into a worldwide legend after its makers' papers had already been planted.
reading: A hoax needs an audience to grow. In 1982 three British authors, Michael Baigent, Richard Leigh and Henry Lincoln, published The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail. They built a large theory on the Priory of Sion papers. The book sold widely and made the Priory famous across the English-speaking world.

In 2003 Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code used the Priory as a central part of its plot. A novel is fiction, and readers know that. But the book's opening pages presented the Priory as real, and many readers took it that way. Tourists began visiting sites linked to the story.

This is how a *legend* can grow from a hoax. A legend is a popular story about the past that is told as if true but cannot be proven. Each retelling cites the one before. After a while, people can point to many books that mention the Priory. None of them leads back to anything older than 1967. Historians call this *circular sourcing*. The sources seem many, but they all rest on the same weak foundation. The test is to follow each claim back, step by step, to its first appearance.

words.d: a popular story about the past told as true but not proven
when many sources seem to agree but all rest on the same original claim
a book that sells a very large number of copies

look.title: How the Priory Story Grew
rows: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail
Plantard admits the story was invented
look.cite: Bibliothèque nationale deposit (1967); Baigent, Leigh and Lincoln (1982); French judicial inquiry (1993); Dan Brown (2003)
look.prompt: The best-known retelling came ten years after the maker's confession. What does that tell you about how corrections travel compared with exciting stories?

check.q: Which 1982 book made the Priory of Sion famous in English?
choices: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail
check.why: Baigent, Leigh and Lincoln's 1982 book built a large theory on the Priory papers.

check.q: What is circular sourcing?
choices: Checking every source against the original
Many sources that seem to agree but all rest on the same original claim
check.why: Circular sourcing makes a claim look well supported when every source leads back to one weak origin.

check.q: How far back can the Priory claims be traced?
check.why: The reading says none of the retellings leads back to anything older than 1967.

lessons.title: A Roll of Film in the Mail
lessons.mainIdea: The Majestic-12 papers first surfaced in 1984 as undeveloped film mailed anonymously, so they had no traceable history.
reading: In December 1984 a television producer named Jaime Shandera received a package. It held a roll of undeveloped 35 mm film and had a New Mexico postmark. There was no return address. When the film was developed, it showed pages of what looked like a top secret government briefing.

The main paper was labeled as a briefing for President-elect Dwight Eisenhower, dated 18 November 1952. It claimed that in 1947 President Harry Truman had set up a secret committee of twelve officials, called Majestic-12 or MJ-12, to handle a crashed flying saucer. The pages looked official, with stamps, code words and signatures.

The papers became public in 1987. A British author, Timothy Good, published them in May of that year, and American researchers William Moore and Shandera released them in the United States. They caused a sensation among people interested in UFOs. Stamps and signatures are easy to copy onto a page.

Notice the provenance. An *anonymous* source, meaning one with no name, mailed a copy of a copy. There was no original paper to examine, no archive file, and no one who admitted sending it. A document with no traceable history is *unauthenticated*: it has not been shown to be what it claims to be.

words.d: with no name given; from an unknown source
not yet shown to be what it claims to be
a short report that gives a leader key information

look.title: MJ-12 Papers: What Year Is It?
rows: Date typed on the Eisenhower briefing
look.cite: Majestic-12 papers (dated 1952); T. Good (1987); FBI file 'Majestic 12', FBI Records: The Vault
look.prompt: The paper says 1952, but the first time anyone can show it existed is 1984. Which date should a historian use as the start of its known history, and why?

check.q: How did the MJ-12 papers first arrive in 1984?
choices: As undeveloped film mailed with no return address
In a sealed letter from Truman
check.why: Shandera received undeveloped 35 mm film in a package with a New Mexico postmark and no return address.

check.q: What did the papers claim Truman did in 1947?
choices: Set up a secret committee of twelve to handle a crashed saucer
check.why: The papers claimed Truman formed Majestic-12 to handle a crashed flying saucer.

check.q: What does unauthenticated mean?
choices: Not yet shown to be what it claims to be
check.why: An unauthenticated document has not been shown to be genuine; the MJ-12 film had no traceable history.

lessons.title: The FBI Checks With the Air Force
lessons.mainIdea: When the FBI asked, Air Force investigators said no Majestic-12 committee had ever been authorized or formed.
reading: Copies of the MJ-12 papers were marked top secret, so the FBI took notice. A document marked classified might mean a real leak of national secrets. The Bureau's file shows that an agent of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations contacted the FBI's Dallas office on 15 September 1988.

The FBI asked the Air Force to check. On 30 November 1988 the Air Force investigators reported back. No such committee, they said, had ever been authorized or formed. A document said to be *classified* is one officially kept secret. This one, the Air Force concluded, was not a real government document at all.

The file also shows the FBI's own reaction. An FBI official wrote that the document was bogus, and the word bogus was written across a copy in the file. Today the FBI posts this file publicly in its online reading room, called the Vault. It was an FBI verdict on a paper, not a secret.

This record is a good example of a *primary source*, a document created at the time by people directly involved. It lets students watch a government agency test a secret document the way a historian would, by asking the office that would have created it.

words.d: officially kept secret by a government
a document created at the time by people directly involved
a person whose job is to find out the facts about something

look.title: The FBI File, in Summary
look.text: In late 1988 Air Force investigators told the FBI that no Majestic-12 committee had ever been authorized or formed, and an FBI official dismissed the document as bogus.
look.cite: Federal Bureau of Investigation, 'Majestic 12' file (1988), FBI Records: The Vault
look.prompt: Why is asking the office that would have created a document a strong test? What might a believer in MJ-12 say in reply?

check.q: What did Air Force investigators tell the FBI on 30 November 1988?
choices: That no such committee had ever been authorized or formed
That MJ-12 was real but still secret
That the film had been lost
check.why: The FBI file records the Air Force's finding that no Majestic-12 committee was ever authorized or formed.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: A modern summary of an event
The most popular book on a topic
A document created at the time by people directly involved
check.why: The FBI's 1988 file is a primary source because it was made at the time by the people investigating.

check.q: Where can the public read the FBI's MJ-12 file today?
choices: In the FBI's online reading room, the Vault
Only in a sealed Air Force vault
check.why: The reading says the FBI posts the file publicly in its online reading room, called the Vault.

lessons.title: The Case For and Against MJ-12
lessons.mainIdea: A few researchers defended the MJ-12 papers, but nearly all investigators judge them forgeries.
reading: Fairness means hearing the defense. The nuclear physicist and UFO researcher Stanton Friedman spent years arguing that the MJ-12 papers might be real. In his 1996 book Top Secret/Majic, he argued that the people named in the papers were real officials and that the details fit their schedules and positions.

Critics answered with several problems. The papers had no provenance: an anonymous roll of film is not an archive. Critics also pointed to features they argued were wrong for real government papers of that time, such as the way dates and markings were written, and a signature they argued had been copied from a genuine letter. And the agency that would have run the committee said it never existed.

Later official reviews found no support either. In March 2024 the Defense Department's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, called AARO, reported on the historical record of government UFO programs. It found no evidence that the government had recovered alien technology. The *consensus*, meaning the broad agreement among experts, is that the MJ-12 papers are forgeries. Using real names does not make a document real. Forgers often borrow real people, because real names make a fake easier to believe.

words.d: broad agreement among experts
a person who judges the strengths and weaknesses of a claim or work
seeming reasonable or possible, though not proven

look.title: A Two-Column Ledger
look.text: For the papers: real officials are named; the details fit their jobs; defenders studied them for years. Against the papers: they came on anonymous film; no original exists; the Air Force said the committee was never formed; critics found problems in dates, markings and a signature; a 2024 review found no evidence of recovered alien technology.
look.prompt: Which single point in the against column would be hardest for a defender to answer? Explain why real names in the for column are weak evidence.

check.q: Which researcher argued for years that the MJ-12 papers might be real?
check.why: Stanton Friedman defended the papers, most fully in his 1996 book Top Secret/Majic.

check.q: Why are real officials' names weak evidence that a document is genuine?
choices: Because real officials never wrote memos
Because the FBI removes names from files
Because forgers often borrow real names to make a fake believable
check.why: The reading says forgers use real names because it makes fakes easier to believe.

check.q: What did the AARO report of March 2024 find?
choices: No evidence that the government recovered alien technology
check.why: AARO's review of the historical record found no evidence of recovered alien technology.

lessons.title: Alternative 3 on British TV
lessons.mainIdea: Alternative 3 was a 1977 British television spoof, written and acted as fiction, about a secret plan to leave a dying Earth.
reading: On 20 June 1977, viewers in Britain watched a program from Anglia Television called Alternative 3. It looked like a serious science documentary. Reporters investigated missing scientists and uncovered a secret plan. The world's powers, it claimed, were preparing to move a chosen few to colonies in space, because Earth was becoming unlivable.

The program was a *spoof*, a humorous imitation of a serious form. It was written by the screenwriter David Ambrose and directed by Christopher Miles. The people on screen were actors playing roles. It had been made to air on 1 April, April Fools' Day, but a labor dispute delayed the broadcast until June.

Moving it from April Fools' Day took away its biggest clue. Some viewers believed what they saw. The program ended with credits listing the writer and the cast, the kind of detail real documentaries also have. But people who missed the ending, or heard about it later, had no way to know. The program is an example of a *mockumentary*, a fictional film made in the style of a documentary. Mockumentaries are a real art form. The problem begins when one is cut loose from its context and passed on as fact.

words.d: a humorous imitation of a serious kind of work
a fictional film made in the style of a documentary
the setting and facts around something that help explain what it means

look.title: Missing Clues
look.text: Imagine seeing Alternative 3 in three ways. Viewer A watches it live on April Fools' Day and sees the credits. Viewer B watches it live in June and turns it off before the credits. Viewer C hears about it from a friend years later.
look.prompt: Which viewer is most likely to believe it is real? List the clues each viewer had or lacked.

check.q: Which station broadcast Alternative 3 in 1977?
check.why: Anglia Television broadcast Alternative 3 on 20 June 1977.

check.q: Why did Alternative 3 air in June instead of on 1 April?
choices: The government banned it in April
A labor dispute delayed the broadcast
It was a live news report
check.why: It was made for April Fools' Day, but a labor dispute pushed the broadcast to June.

check.q: What is a mockumentary?
choices: A fictional film made in the style of a documentary
A real documentary about fake news
check.why: Alternative 3 was a mockumentary: fiction made to look like a documentary.

lessons.title: How a Spoof Became a Claim
lessons.mainIdea: After 1977, Alternative 3 was retold in a book and then repeated in conspiracy writing as if it were a real exposé.
reading: In 1978 a writer named Leslie Watkins published a book version of Alternative 3. The book kept the documentary style. On a shelf, it looked like nonfiction. Each new form carried the story further from its first context as an April Fools' spoof. Its readers did not see a cast list.

Over the next years, the story's claims appeared in conspiracy books and talks as evidence of a real secret plan. Bill Cooper, whose 1991 book Behold a Pale Horse this course studies in Unit 17, was one of the writers who repeated Alternative 3 as if it described real events. The show's credits and its writer's name did not travel with the claims.

This is sometimes called *context collapse*. A piece of content is removed from the setting that explained it, and a new audience reads it without the clues. A joke, a novel or a drama can then look like a leak. The claim has not become stronger. It has only lost its label.

The fix is to trace the claim upstream, meaning back toward its first source. Follow Alternative 3 back through the books and talks, and it ends at a television studio, a script and a cast list. That first appearance is its *origin*, and it answers the question.

words.d: when content is removed from the setting that explained it and read by a new audience without clues
the first source or starting point of something
back toward the first source of a claim

look.title: Tracing a Claim Upstream
look.text: Step 4: A post says a secret plan to move the elite into space was exposed on television. Step 3: A conspiracy book repeats the plan as fact. Step 2: A 1978 book tells the story in documentary style. Step 1: A 1977 television spoof with a writer, a director and a cast of actors.
look.prompt: At which step was the fiction label lost? What single question would take a reader from Step 4 back to Step 1?

check.q: Who wrote the 1978 book version of Alternative 3?
check.why: Leslie Watkins wrote the 1978 book version, which kept the documentary style.

check.q: What is context collapse?
choices: When content loses the setting that explained it and reaches a new audience without clues
When a court overturns a verdict
check.why: Context collapse is how Alternative 3 lost its label as a spoof and was read as fact.

check.q: Where does Alternative 3 lead when traced upstream?
choices: To a 1977 television script and cast list
check.why: Tracing it back ends at Anglia's 1977 program, with its writer, director and actors.

lessons.title: Four Tests for Any Document
lessons.mainIdea: Historians test a document by its provenance, its physical materials, its anachronisms, and who gains from it.
reading: Historians use a set of tests on any document that seems too good to be true. The first is provenance. Where did this come from, and who has held it? A letter kept in a family's papers for 150 years, then given to an archive, has strong provenance. A roll of film from an unknown sender has almost none.

The second test is the material itself. Paper, parchment, ink and typewriter type all change over time. Experts can often date a page by what it is made of and how its letters were printed. Checking whether a document is genuine is called *authentication*. The MJ-12 papers could not be tested this way, because only photographs existed.

The third test looks for an *anachronism*, something placed in the wrong time. A word, a title, a date format or an object that did not yet exist can expose a forgery at once. Forgers know the big facts of the past, but they often slip on the small ones.

The fourth test asks who gains. Who benefits if people believe this? Plantard gained a royal family tree. Promoters gained sales and attention. A benefit does not prove a document false, but it tells you where to look harder. Together, these tests turn a feeling of doubt into evidence.

words.d: the process of checking whether a document is genuine
something placed in a time where it does not belong
a reason a person has for doing something

look.title: Match the Test
look.text: Clue 1: The document arrived by anonymous mail. Clue 2: The paper contains a kind of fiber first made decades after the date on the page. Clue 3: A letter dated 1850 mentions a telephone call. Clue 4: The document names its finder as the heir to a lost throne.
look.prompt: Match each clue to one of the four tests: provenance, material, anachronism, or who gains. Which clue alone would be enough to prove a forgery?

check.q: What does the provenance test ask?
choices: Where the document came from and who has held it
check.why: Provenance is a document's known history of origin and custody.

check.q: Why could the MJ-12 papers not pass the material test?
choices: Only photographs existed, not original paper
They were too old to test
check.why: The reading says only photographs existed, so the paper and ink could not be examined.

check.q: A letter dated 1850 mentions a telephone call. Which test does this fail?
check.why: A telephone in an 1850 letter is something placed in a time before it existed, an anachronism.

lessons.title: A Real Find: The Chinon Parchment
lessons.mainIdea: The Chinon Parchment, found in the Vatican archives in 2001, passes the tests, but it proves less than some headlines claimed.
reading: Not every surprising document is fake. In September 2001 an Italian scholar, Barbara Frale, was working in the Vatican archives. She identified a parchment that had been misfiled for centuries. A catalog entry from 1628 had mentioned it, but too vaguely for anyone to find it. It recorded questioning of the Knights Templar at Chinon, in France.

The parchment is dated 17 to 20 August 1308. It records that three cardinals, sent by Pope Clement V, questioned the Templar Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, and other leaders. The cardinals *absolved* them, meaning they formally forgave them of sin and restored them to the Church's sacraments.

Compare its tests with the planted papers. Its provenance is strong: it sat in the pope's own archive for about seven centuries. Its material is a medieval parchment. Its contents fit other records of the Templar trials. It gave no one a throne or a fortune. In 2007 the Vatican published a facsimile, a careful exact copy, of the trial documents.

But a genuine document can still be overstated. Some headlines said the pope had declared the Templars innocent. The parchment does not say that. It did not end the case. The order was still suppressed in 1312, and Molay was burned in 1314. Reading carefully means claiming only what the *document* shows.

words.d: formally forgiven of sin by church authority
a careful, exact copy of a document
a written or printed record that gives information or evidence
put in the wrong place in a set of records

look.title: The Chinon Parchment Through Time
look.cite: Chinon Parchment, Vatican Apostolic Archive; Processus contra Templarios (Vatican, 2007)
look.prompt: The Dossiers Secrets have a known history starting in 1967. How long is the Chinon Parchment's known history? How does that difference affect how much we trust each one?

check.q: Who identified the Chinon Parchment in 2001?
check.why: Barbara Frale identified the misfiled parchment in the Vatican archives in September 2001.

check.q: What does the parchment record the cardinals doing in 1308?
choices: Absolving Molay and other Templar leaders
check.why: The cardinals absolved the leaders, forgiving them of sin and restoring them to the sacraments.

check.q: Why is the claim that the parchment proves the Templars innocent an overstatement?
choices: Because the parchment is a forgery
Because Frale later admitted making it
Because it records absolution but did not end the case; the order was still suppressed in 1312
Because it was found in a Paris library
check.why: The parchment is genuine, but it records forgiveness, not a verdict of innocence, and the order was still suppressed.

lessons.title: Try It Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: Students can apply the four tests to a practice document and explain their verdict with evidence.
reading: Now it is your turn to be the historian. Below is a practice document. It is invented for this lesson, so you can test it without harm. Your job is not to guess. Your job is to find evidence and explain it. Take your time; careful work matters more than speed. Read the whole document once before you begin testing it.

Work through the tests in order. For provenance, ask who found it and how it reached them. For material, ask what it is written on and how. For anachronism, read every date, word and object slowly. For who gains, ask who benefits if people believe it. Write one sentence of evidence for each test.

Then reach a *verdict*, a judgment based on evidence. Historians use three honest labels. A document can be authenticated, meaning shown to be genuine. It can be shown false, meaning evidence proves it is not what it claims. Or it can be *unverified*, meaning there is not yet enough evidence either way. Remember the lesson of Chinon. A strange document is not automatically fake, and a real document is not automatically proof of everything people claim. Good judgment stays close to the evidence, in both directions.

words.d: a judgment reached after weighing the evidence
not yet checked or proven either way
shown by evidence to be genuine

look.title: Practice Document (Invented for This Lesson)
look.text: A typed page, found last month in an attic box by a man selling a book about his family. It reads: Secret Order of the Lantern, minutes of 4 July 1846. Members present: twelve. Our grand master, an ancestor of the finder, reports that the order's gold is hidden near the river. Send replies to our lodge, ZIP code 60601.
look.prompt: Apply all four tests. ZIP codes began in the United States in 1963. What is your verdict, and which piece of evidence decides it?

check.q: In the practice document, which detail is an anachronism?
choices: A ZIP code in a document dated 1846
check.why: ZIP codes began in 1963, so one could not appear in minutes dated 1846.

check.q: Which test does the finder's book about his family raise?
check.why: The finder benefits if people believe his ancestor led a secret order, so the who-gains test applies.

check.q: What does unverified mean as a verdict?
choices: Not yet enough evidence either way
check.why: Unverified means the evidence does not yet settle the question in either direction.

review.q: What made the Dossiers Secrets seem official?
choices: They had a call number in France's national library
review.why: Being deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale gave them a catalog number and borrowed authority.

review.q: Which piece of evidence most directly shows the Priory of Sion story was invented?
choices: Its list of famous grand masters
Tourist visits to sites in the story
review.why: The maker's own sworn confession is direct evidence that the Priory claims were invented.

review.q: Why did the MJ-12 papers have weak provenance?
choices: They arrived as anonymous film with no original paper
They were printed in a newspaper
review.why: An anonymous roll of film is a copy of a copy, with no traceable history.

review.q: What did Air Force investigators report to the FBI about Majestic-12?
choices: That no such committee had ever been authorized or formed
review.why: The FBI file records the Air Force's finding that no such committee ever existed.

choices: A French forgery in a library
A 1977 television spoof with a writer, director and actors
review.why: Anglia Television made it as a spoof documentary, first meant for April Fools' Day.

review.q: A letter dated 1790 mentions a railroad station. Which test does it fail?
review.why: A railroad station in 1790 is something placed in a time before it existed.

review.q: How does the Chinon Parchment differ from the planted papers?
choices: It was first a TV spoof
It has strong provenance in the Vatican archive for about seven centuries
review.why: The parchment stayed in the pope's own archive and fits other trial records.

review.q: Which statement about the Chinon Parchment is accurate?
choices: It proves the pope declared the Templars innocent
It is a forgery by Plantard
It was found by the FBI
It records that cardinals absolved the Templar leaders in 1308, though the order was still suppressed
review.why: It records absolution, not a verdict of innocence, and the order was suppressed in 1312.
